Notes: Earliest Judean documented in the city of Nippur itself: sale of two female slaves by the Judean Banā-Yāma in Nippur (N 4518, unpublished tablet, Penn Museum; dated 22-XII-? Darius I, 521-486 BCE; year = midpoint, c.). Presence of an individual; no community size. Year Established -597 basis: the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia ('Nippur') states that 'the principal colony of the Hebrew exiles of 597 B.C. was planted beside the canal Chebar (Kabar) not far from Nippur' (cf. Ezekiel 1:1-3, 3:15); Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Chebar') identifies the Chebar with the Shatt el-Nil passing Nippur, a canal named in the Murashu documents. This is a regional (Nippur countryside) attestation, not the city. Source: T. Alstola, Judeans in Babylonia (Brill 2020, open access), p. 235 n. 1194 (citing Zadok 2014a). [Review fix: Year Established changed from -597 to -503: earliest Judean documented in the city of Nippur itself (slave sale, 521-486 BCE); the 597 BCE exiles were settled in the region "not far from Nippur", not in the city]

Earliest Judean in the Murašû archive: a Judean attested in the second earliest text of the archive, BE 9 3, 13th year of Artaxerxes I (452 BCE). Alstola stresses that the Murašûs lived in Nippur but 'their Judean clients inhabited the surrounding countryside' (Nippur region villages, not the city). Alstola 2020, pp. 45-46, 167.

Judean Pili-Yāma/Šillimu witnessed three documents in Nippur on the same day (BE 9 34; IMT 7, 8), 34th year of Artaxerxes I (431 BCE); Alstola notes he was 'often present in Nippur' and that Judean witnesses were asked to witness documents 'when they were available in Nippur' - i.e. Judeans visiting the city from the countryside, not necessarily residents. Alstola 2020, pp. 168, 180, 207.

Lease BE 9 45 (written in Nippur, 20-V-36 Artaxerxes I = 429 BCE): Enlil-šum-iddin (Murašû) leases the Urâti canal and lands to the Judean Yadi-Yāma, his three sons, another Judean and four others 'and their anonymous colleagues' of the village of Bīt-Gērāya for an annual rent of 700 kurru of barley, two oxen and twenty sheep. Alstola concludes Bīt-Gērāya was a village in the Nippur countryside 'inhabited by people of Judean and generally non-Babylonian origin' - a community of farmers. No population figure. Alstola 2020, pp. 172-180.

Summary of the Murašû evidence: 'Altogether 61 Judean individuals appear in 64 different documents' of an archive of c. 730 texts covering 454-404 BCE (year = midpoint, c.). Population left blank: 61 is the number of individuals attested in one firm's business records, not the size of the Judean population of Nippur or its region. Alstola finds the chronological distribution shows 'no major changes occurred among the Judean population in the Nippur region in the last half of the fifth century' and Judean socio-economic status no different from other deportees (farmers/landholders in the land-for-service sector; a few minor officials, one sēpiru and one šaknu). Alstola 2020, pp. 164-169, 206.

Secondary summary (J. Brumbach, Kesher journal): Murašû texts dated 455-403 BCE (year = midpoint, c.); citing J. D. Purvis, documents 'testify to the existence of Jewish communities in 28 settlements in the Nippur area'; citing W. Schniedewind, the texts 'mention about eighty distinctively Jewish personal names'; Coogan: Jews appear 'as agriculturists, fishermen, sheepherders, and co-creditors of contracts'. Regional figures (28 settlements, ~80 names) - not a population count of Nippur; Population blank.

Onomastic data on Judeans in the Murašû archive (Levavi 2024, Aula Orientalis 42/1, table 1 based on Alstola 2020): 66% (40/60) of Judean protagonists bear Yahwistic names vs 46% (19/41) of their fathers; 22% of Judean patronyms are Akkadian. Most tablets date 439-417 BCE (year = midpoint, c.). The 60 protagonists are named individuals, not a population count; Population blank.

Alstola notes 'significant Judean habitation in the village of Ashkelon near Nippur in the late fifth century' (late 5th c. BCE, year c. -425), a twin town named after deportees' origin in the Nippur countryside; shows Judeans living in mixed villages around Nippur. No figure. Alstola 2020, p. 272.

Peak of Murašû documents pertaining to Judeans: eleven texts in the 4th year of Darius II (420 BCE), with Judeans as witnesses, minor officials, landholders and creditors in the Nippur region. Alstola considers the peak incidental. Alstola 2020, pp. 168-169.

Last Judean attested in the Murašû archive: PBS 2/1 148 (late Aršam group), 11th year of Darius II (413 BCE). Alstola: the archive 'attests to the presence of a lively Judean community in the Nippur region almost two centuries after the deportations from Judah'; after this 'a substantial break of any textual evidence' until Jewish communities reappear in Babylonia in the 1st c. CE (gap in evidence, not documented absence). Alstola 2020, pp. 167, 276.

Tablet TuM 2-3 123 (8th year of Artaxerxes II or III, i.e. 397 or 351 BCE; year = midpoint, c.): commodities owed by the Judean Zakar-Yāma/Sepā-Yāma to be delivered in Nippur; his ring seal impressed; place of writing broken. Latest Judean attestation connected with Nippur in the period found. Alstola 2020, p. 235 n. 1193 (citing Zadok 2002).
